analysis.investment_thesis: Dr. Agarwal's fails both Magic Formula tests: Earnings Yield of ~3.1% (EBIT ₹463 Cr / EV ~₹14,932 Cr) is far below my 6% minimum, and ROCE of 9.99% signals the business doesn't yet earn high returns on the capital it is aggressively deploying. Paying 110x earnings for a company with 4.76% ROE is the opposite of what the Magic Formula demands.
key_strengths: Strong revenue growth: 26.4% CAGR over 5 years (₹531→₹1,711 Cr), showing real demand for eye-care services
Operating CF consistently positive all 5 years; operating income CAGR of 30.1% shows improving unit economics
Niche healthcare moat in eye-care with defensible brand and repeat-procedure volumes (cataract, refractive)
key_risks: Earnings Yield of 3.1% — massively overvalued by Magic Formula standards; EV/EBITDA 31x, P/E 110x leave zero margin of safety
FCF collapsing: capex surged to ₹321 Cr in FY25 leaving only ₹40 Cr FCF vs ₹118 Cr prior year — capital voracious expansion destroys near-term returns
Thin profitability: net margin ~6.4%, ROE only 4.76%, ROCE 9.99% — business is not yet earning above its cost of capital despite years of growth
red_flags: Earnings Yield of 3.1% — well below my 6% floor; Magic Formula rank would be in bottom decile on valuation
Net profit was negative in FY20 (−₹21 Cr) and FY21 (−₹59 Cr); profitability is nascent and fragile
Investing CF of −₹750 Cr in FY25 on only ₹360 Cr operating CF — company is consuming more than it generates, relying on equity/debt raises
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Magic Formula math is unambiguous here. EBIT of ₹463 Cr against an Enterprise Value of ~₹14,932 Cr (Market Cap ₹14,075 Cr + Net Debt ~₹857 Cr) gives an Earnings Yield of just 3.1% — I want to see 12%+ for a compelling buy. On the quality side, ROCE of 9.99% and ROE of 4.76% tell me the business is not yet a high-return compounder; it is in heavy-investment mode where capital is being consumed faster than returns are being generated. Capex has ballooned to ₹321 Cr in FY25, absorbing nearly 90% of operating cash flow and leaving only ₹40 Cr in free cash flow — a sharp deterioration from ₹118 Cr the prior year.

The underlying business has real secular tailwinds (India's massive under-served eye-care population, aging demographics) and the revenue trajectory is genuinely impressive. But the Magic Formula is agnostic to stories — it asks: are you cheap AND good today? The answer is no on both counts. At 110x trailing earnings and 31x EV/EBITDA, the market has already priced in a decade of flawless execution. I require a margin of safety the current price simply does not offer. Until capex investment matures into meaningfully higher ROCE (>20%) and the earnings yield compresses below 8-9% EV multiples, this remains firmly in "avoid" territory.
